title: A proof that quantum polynomial time exceeds classical polynomial time on decision problems

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a mathematical proof that an explicit yes-or-no problem can be solved efficiently by a quantum computer but cannot be solved efficiently by any randomized classical computer. The precise target is a problem in BQP but outside BPP: BQP allows quantum polynomial-time computation with bounded error, while BPP allows randomized classical polynomial-time computation with bounded error. This sets a stronger target than merely proving that the problem lies outside deterministic classical polynomial time, P. The supplied 2025 paper identifies the BQP-versus-BPP separation as unproved at that time.

Scope clarification: the strongest version of this goal requires an unconditional proof about ordinary computation, without an oracle or unproved hardness assumptions. An assumption-dependent theorem could be valuable progress, but its assumptions would remain part of the conclusion. The target concerns decision problems; sampling distributions, computing functions and finding witnesses are related tasks with different success conditions. Requiring every answer to have an efficiently checkable certificate would add a separate constraint and is not part of the decision-problem target adopted here.

significance.text: Such a proof would establish an intrinsic mathematical difference between efficient quantum and randomized classical computation. Its force would come from ruling out every classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm for the chosen problem, including algorithms not yet invented. The supplied paper motivates reducing or removing conjectures as a route toward establishing this fundamental distinction, while its own results stop short of the proposed decision-problem theorem.

Interpretive significance: the result would become a permanent part of the mathematical account of computational possibility. Calling it a new law of computation conveys that foundational ambition, but comparisons with calculus or universal computation are historical judgments, not technical consequences of a separation theorem. The direct achievement would be a proof of an asymptotic computational distinction.

Conditional impact assessment: practical consequences would depend on the problem separated, its algorithms and the machines capable of running them. A theorem alone would not provide useful runtime constants, fault-tolerant hardware, a cryptographic attack or a molecular-design method. A factoring-based separation could sharpen the theoretical basis for quantum cryptanalysis, but attacking deployed keys would still require a suitable implementation at the relevant scale. An oracle separation or conditional sampling-hardness result would contribute evidence and theory without meeting this unconditional decision-problem goal.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a proof combining two statements about the same explicit decision problem: an efficient bounded-error quantum algorithm exists, and no bounded-error randomized classical polynomial-time algorithm exists. Demonstrating a quantum algorithm or defeating selected classical implementations establishes only part of that claim. The supplied paper documents the absence of a BQP-versus-BPP proof in 2025 and develops conditional sampling and functional results instead.

Scientific synthesis: the central obstacle is a classical computational lower bound strong enough to cover all randomized polynomial-time algorithms. It must address the actual decision problem without relying on an oracle or assuming the hardness that the theorem is meant to establish. If the route begins with sampling, function computation or search, it must also supply a rigorous connection to a decision problem that preserves the required efficiency and hardness. The supplied evidence does not identify a technique that overcomes these obstacles.

The 2025 result illustrates why stronger conditional evidence still leaves the central breakthrough missing. For the approximate sampling tasks considered, the paper strengthens the consequence of efficient classical sampling from a collapse of the polynomial hierarchy to its third level to a collapse to its second level, while retaining the respective additional conjectures. This is a substantive improvement in the conditional argument, not an unconditional lower bound for a decision problem. The review also records that the paper describes its main proof as nonrelativizing; being conditional and being relativized are distinct limitations.

current_state.text: Simon C. Marshall, Scott Aaronson and Vedran Dunjko published Improved Separation Between Quantum and Classical Computers for Sampling and Functional Tasks at the 40th Computational Complexity Conference on 29 July 2025, in LIPIcs volume 339, article 5, pages 5:1–5:14. As documented in the supplied review, the paper states that a formal BQP-versus-BPP separation had not been proved. This establishes a dated position in the supplied literature; it does not establish the field's status on 1 November 2026.

The paper shows that efficient classical approximate sampling for BosonSampling, IQP or DQC1 would imply collapse of the polynomial hierarchy to its second level, subject to the respective additional conjectures. Earlier results gave a third-level collapse. The paper also derives a conditional separation for functional tasks. These conclusions strengthen the theoretical case for quantum advantage while preserving both the assumptions and the distinction between sampling, functions and decision problems. They do not prove BQP differs from BPP.

Evidence boundary: the supplied review reports internally verified source identity and a complete, untruncated 14-page PDF, with no recorded extraction issues; the source index also lists an untruncated HTML artifact. The limitation is therefore the scope and date of the evidence, rather than a reported access failure. The freshness search record is empty, so this record cannot characterize the cited paper as the latest or strongest result available in November 2026.

Methodological assessment: experimental sampling or out-of-time-order correlator observations alone would not prove the proposed asymptotic decision-class separation. Finite experiments test particular devices, sizes and classical comparisons; the target theorem rules out every randomized classical polynomial-time algorithm. No experimental sampling or OTOC evidence is supplied here, so no particular experimental achievement or dispute is assessed. The earlier research also invokes Shor's algorithm, but the supplied review says the cited paper does not document that algorithm; it is therefore not treated here as a separately verified achievement.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed mathematical criterion: provide an explicit decision problem, a rigorous proof that it belongs to BQP and a rigorous proof that it lies outside BPP, without an oracle or unproved hardness assumptions. The formulation should specify valid inputs, the yes/no condition, the input-size measure and the bounded-error guarantee. A theorem proved under named assumptions would remain a qualified advance rather than satisfy this strongest completion criterion.
completion_criteria.label: Unconditional proof of explicit decision problem in BQP outside BPP

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation milestone: a refereed, accepted proof in a standard theory venue, accompanied by enough detail for independent experts to reconstruct and check both the quantum algorithm and the classical lower bound. Publication acceptance is a proposed milestone, not an established certification standard or a substitute for mathematical correctness. Any reduction connecting a different task type to the decision problem must be explicit and preserve the relevant polynomial-time bounds.
completion_criteria.label: Accepted refereed proof with reconstructible algorithm and classical lower bound

completion_criteria.text: Conditional factoring route: assuming the quantum polynomial-time factoring capability invoked in the earlier research, a suitable route would define an explicit decision problem whose answers allow factors to be recovered with polynomial-time overhead. One would then need a proof that factoring is outside randomized classical polynomial time to rule out BPP algorithms for that decision problem. Merely proving factoring outside deterministic P would not establish the stronger BQP-versus-BPP target. The supplied evidence does not document the quantum factoring algorithm or provide the required decision reduction, so this remains a qualified route rather than a verified completion example.
completion_criteria.label: Quantum factoring decision problem with polynomial recovery outside BPP

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: correctness checks and numerical examples may help expose mistakes, but finite tests cannot establish an asymptotic complexity separation. Even a valid separation would concern the specified problem and computational model; it would not show that quantum computers outperform classical computers on every task or at every input size. Practical usefulness would require separate evidence about resource costs, hardware and relevant problem instances.
completion_criteria.label: Stated limits of finite tests, problem scope, and practical usefulness

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: QUA-01, Distance-scalable universal fault-tolerant quantum computation, concerns reliable execution of general quantum algorithms. QUA-07 concerns proving a mathematical limit on classical computation. Reliable hardware could make a separating algorithm executable, but hardware demonstrations and complexity lower bounds establish different things.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-02, Cryptographically relevant execution of Shor’s algorithm, concerns carrying out a specific algorithm at a practically consequential scale. It overlaps the qualified factoring route described above. Successful execution would not itself prove that every randomized classical polynomial-time factoring algorithm is impossible, while a separation theorem would not itself demonstrate cryptographically relevant execution.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-03, Experimentally confirmed quantum prediction of sign-problematic matter, concerns a specific scientific prediction and its experimental confirmation. QUA-09, An end-to-end superpolynomial quantum speedup on large classical data, concerns an application-level computational advantage including the surrounding workflow. Either could motivate complexity questions, but evidence of performance on finite instances would not by itself establish QUA-07's unrestricted classical lower bound.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-04, A laboratory material that stores a logical qubit passively at nonzero temperature, and QUA-05, Universal computation by braiding non-Abelian anyons, concern physical storage and computational mechanisms. They could support the physical realization of quantum computation, but neither capability entails a proof that BQP differs from BPP.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-06, Fault-tolerant quantum interconnects that let processors scale by adding modules, QUA-08, Local, universal fault tolerance whose overhead stays bounded as the error falls, and QUA-10, Foundry-made fault-tolerant quantum computation without a dilution refrigerator, address scaling, error-correction overhead and fabrication or operating conditions. These remain separate engineering advances. Their success could improve implementation prospects without settling the mathematical separation, and QUA-07 would not establish their feasibility.

brief.title: A proven limit that quantum computers can surpass
possible: You could have a yes-or-no question that a quantum computer answers efficiently, with a controlled chance of error, knowing that no ordinary computer could match that efficiency—even using randomness. The proof would cover every classical algorithm, including ones nobody has invented.
why: For researchers, this would establish a permanent mathematical difference between quantum and classical computing. It would show that the advantage comes from the computational model itself, rather than from a temporary lead over known software.

sources.who: Simon C. Marshall, Scott Aaronson and Vedran Dunjko
sources.showed: They strengthened conditional arguments against efficient classical sampling: generating outputs with specified probabilities. Classical success would compress a hierarchy of classical problem classes to its second level, under unproved assumptions.
sources.quote:
These results are an improvement over
previous work which either achieved a collapse to the third level or were concerned with exact
sampling, a physically impractical case.
sources.cited_for: Their theorem strengthens conditional evidence for quantum advantages in sampling and computing functions.
sources.not_established: It does not prove an unconditional advantage for a yes-or-no problem.

sources.showed: Shor gave efficient quantum algorithms for factoring integers—finding their prime factors—and discrete logarithms, another number-theory problem.
sources.quote:
Eﬃcient randomized alg orithms are given for
these two problems on a hypothetical quantum computer.
sources.cited_for: Factoring has an efficient quantum algorithm, making it a possible route to the desired proof.
sources.not_established: The work does not rule out an efficient randomized classical factoring algorithm.

sources.showed: They proved a quantum advantage in a black-box model, where computers query a subroutine without access to its code. The classical limitation covers a hierarchy broader than efficient randomized computation.
sources.quote:
More precisely, we give an explicit black-box (promise) problem, that can be solved by a
polynomial-time quantum algorithm with only one query, but cannot be solved by a classical
algorithm in the polynomial-time hierarchy.
sources.cited_for: A rigorous quantum advantage is possible with black-box access.
sources.not_established: The separation depends on black-box access and does not establish the target for ordinary computation.

sources.showed: For a problem called Forrelation, they proved an essentially optimal gap between quantum and randomized classical query counts: how often an algorithm accesses its input.
sources.quote:
We achieve essentially the largest possible separation between quan tum and classical query
complexities.
sources.cited_for: Forrelation provides a proven quantum advantage in input access.
sources.not_established: A gap in input queries does not establish the required gap in total computation time.

sources.who: Scott Aaronson, Shalev Ben-David and Robin Kothari
sources.showed: They built a yes-or-no problem defined for every input and proved a quantum advantage in input queries, even when both kinds of algorithm may make errors.
sources.quote:
We present the ﬁrst super-quadratic separation between qua ntum and classical query complexity
when both models are allowed bounded error.
sources.cited_for: Proven query advantages also exist for problems defined on every input.
sources.not_established: The result concerns input queries rather than an unconditional separation in efficient computation.

shown: Shor proved that quantum computers can factor efficiently. Raz and Tal proved a separation with black-box access. Marshall, Aaronson and Dunjko strengthened conditional results for sampling and computing functions. These achievements leave the unconditional yes-or-no target open.
missing: A specific yes-or-no problem with an efficient quantum algorithm and a proof that every efficient randomized classical algorithm fails.
A classical impossibility proof that uses neither unproved hardness assumptions nor a black-box subroutine.
For routes through sampling, computing functions or finding factors, a rigorous connection preserving efficiency and hardness for a yes-or-no problem.

milestones.label: An unconditional quantum advantage for a specified yes-or-no problem
milestones.explanation: A proof would establish an efficient quantum algorithm and rule out every efficient randomized classical algorithm for the same precisely defined problem. It would require no unproved assumptions or black-box subroutine.

milestones.label: An accepted proof that independent experts can reconstruct
milestones.explanation: A refereed proof would be accepted at a standard theory venue, with enough detail to reconstruct the algorithm and classical impossibility argument. This would support independent scrutiny of both halves.

milestones.label: A factoring decision problem beyond efficient classical computation
milestones.explanation: A specified yes-or-no problem would allow efficient recovery of factors, with factoring proved beyond efficient randomized classical computation. Combined with quantum factoring, this would establish the separation.

milestones.label: Clear limits on tests, scope and practical usefulness
milestones.explanation: The result would state why finite tests cannot prove its claim about growing inputs, and define its scope and practical limits. This would distinguish the mathematical advantage from useful performance on actual hardware.

uncertain: Which explicit yes-or-no problem could support a proof against every efficient randomized classical algorithm?
Could factoring provide the route, or would a different problem make the classical impossibility proof more tractable?
Would the separated problem yield a useful advantage once hardware and resource costs are included?
